subject: estimate.missing with PLS regression may be reflecting

messages.author: 2c7106159c8e6d5b
messages.subject: estimate.missing with PLS regression may be reflecting
parts:
Hi there,

I was putting together a demonstration of the estimate.missing function--knocking out one landmark, showing the imputed estimate with the TPS and regression alternatives. I think my outcome from PLS regression shows a complete reflection of the estimated specimen. TPS works fine. 

You can see it clearly in the snout (incidentally, the location of the knocked out landmark) in the attached image. However, it's not just there. I spent awhile comparing the regression-imputed shape to the true shape in an rgl window. All the asymmetries have flipped. 

Best, David

messages.author: 4d71c6e24fb21497
messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] estimate.missing with PLS regression may be reflecting
parts:
David and the group,

 

This is an interesting case. Essentially, the multiple aspects of symmetry in the shapes are confusing the PLS algorithm. This can happen, but having a way to catch it is hard.

 

However, this example emphasizes an important point: landmark estimation really needs to be used NOT as a black box, but rather with frequent inspection of the estimated shapes; as David has done here. In many cases, the PLS-regression is generally better, but not always. This is a case of the not always.

 

Dean

 

Dr. Dean C. Adams

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] estimate.missing with PLS regression may be reflecting
parts:
Makes sense. As long as you inspect you could always reflect back the result, but it wouldn't even matter for many types of analysis (directional asymmetry and attempts to correlate facial shape with other sided features would be obvious exceptions). 

Thank you, Dean

David
